terms.gloss: a debate, the arguing out of a disputed point
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.34: ūnum per disceptātiōnem, alterum per vim
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “good prose”, and the word Cicero prefers in his speeches.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; dē and the ablative
evidence: Liv. 21.19.1: dē foederum jūre verbīs disceptāre
Traupman 177: Dē quō disceptātum est?, What was the debate about?

terms.gloss: a sharp exchange of words, as in the senate
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “a strife or contest in words … with or without passion”; Cicero uses it in his letters and dialogues for heated exchanges, such as his clash with Clodius in the senate.

phrases.latin: nam cum sint duo genera dēcertandī, ūnum per disceptātiōnem, alterum per vim, cumque illud proprium sit hominis, hoc bēluārum, cōnfugiendum est ad posterius, sī ūtī nōn licet superiōre
phrases.english: for there are two ways of settling a dispute, one by debate and the other by force, and since the first belongs to man and the second to beasts, we may resort to the second only if we cannot use the first

sources: Lewis & Short: disceptatio · Lewis & Short: discepto · Lewis & Short: altercatio
